newsitem.title: USA: Rubin sees U.S. House upholding China MFN.
newsitem.headline: Rubin sees U.S. House upholding China MFN.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Thursday he believed that the House of Representatives would uphold President Clinton's decision to renew China's trade status, but that the vote would be closer than last year.
"My best guess in the final analysis is the House will not vote to revoke MFN (Most Favored Nation trade status)," Rubin told reporters following a speech to the U.S.-China Business Council.
Rubin said he did not have a vote count on the MFN issue.
"All I can say is I think it is going to be more difficult by a fair bit because of all the forces at work," Rubin said.
Conservative and liberal groups concerned about human rights abuses, labor issues, nuclear technology proliferation and other issues have joined forces to oppose renewal of China's MFN trade status.
But Rubin said he believed that the administration would prevail in fighting off efforts to revoke MFN.
"In the final analysis, I think we will succeed," Rubin said.
The House is expected to vote first on the China MFN issue. Last year the Senate never voted on China MFN status after it was upheld in the House by a wide margin.

Rubin was also asked about an increase in May in Japan's trade surplus. He said many people had been expecting a rise in Japan's surplus and it was a question of whether it will be sustained or short-lived.
"That's what we've got to wait and see," he said.
Japan said on Thursday it posted a customs-cleared trade surplus of 41.16 billion yen in the first 20 days of May, compared with a deficit of 180.94 billion yen the same period a year earlier.
